name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,174

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, enumeration length); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing; the grid proves the blog's answer wrong at 18 down, corrected here

clue.text: Rough breeches worn by a king

indicators.note: clothing that is worn wraps around its wearer, so the garment goes round the other piece

blocks.note: hose are old-fashioned breeches or leggings
taken as written
R, for Rex, is the standard abbreviation for a king

explanation.surface: A monarch dressed in coarse, scratchy breeches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough' looks like a description of the cloth, but it is the definition, in its sense of a rasping voice. A R sits inside HOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough voice is a hoarse one: harsh, grating and croaky, as after shouting or a cold.

clue.text: Parish boy, short of meat

blocks.note: to be short is to have nothing, and O is the zero or nothing figure
liver is offal eaten as meat

explanation.surface: The workhouse orphan who famously went hungry and asked for more.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickens subtitled Oliver Twist 'The Parish Boy's Progress'. The surface recalls Oliver's empty bowl, while the wordplay gives O, nothing, before LIVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's hero Oliver Twist is a pauper raised by the parish workhouse, the original parish boy of the novel's subtitle.

clue.text: Hurt, lifting stuff

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting something lets it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to mar is to damage or spoil

explanation.surface: Someone straining a muscle while heaving heavy things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stuff' reads as a noun, the things being lifted, but it is a verb meaning to cram.
explanation.definitionFit: To ram something in is to force or cram it, the same action as stuffing a container full.

clue.text: Sign leaving Kent perhaps: ‘Witch lived here’

indicators.note: whatever leaves is no longer present, so those letters drop out

blocks.note: to endorse a cheque is to sign it
Kent is a county in South-East England, abbreviated SE

explanation.surface: A road sign at the edge of Kent warning of a local witch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign' looks like a noun, a road sign, but it is the verb ENDORSE. Kent is an English county in the South-East.
explanation.definitionFit: In the First Book of Samuel, King Saul consults the Witch of Endor, who summons up the prophet Samuel's ghost.

clue.text: Lover, in case he left the wife of his youth

definitions.text: he left the wife of his youth
definitions.note: a description of the author by the book he wrote

indicators.note: one thing placed in another ends up enclosed by it

blocks.note: a nut is a fanatic or lover of something
a chest is a large box or case

explanation.surface: A lover who has abandoned the woman he married when young.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks like desertion, but here it means left behind as a legacy: Charles W. Chesnutt, African American author, wrote 'The Wife of His Youth' (1899).
explanation.definitionFit: Chesnutt's best-known story collection is The Wife of His Youth, so he is the writer who left posterity that book.

clue.text: Drink spiked by university conspirator …

indicators.note: spiking means slipping an extra ingredient secretly into something

blocks.note: cassis is a blackcurrant liqueur
U is the usual abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A plotter at college slipping something into someone's drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Cassius is the 'lean and hungry' plotter against Caesar in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaius Cassius Longinus led the plot to assassinate Julius Caesar, so he is a conspirator by historical record.

clue.text: … it’s one used for sex

blocks.note: surface reading: following the spiked drink, a hint at something used to get sex
setter's reading: 'it' is itself a coy stand-in word for sex, so the clue names a polite substitute expression

explanation.surface: Continuing the spiked drink of the previous clue, a sinister hint at a date-rape drug.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis ties this to the spiked drink, suggesting a drug. In fact 'it' as in 'doing it' is the classic example of the answer, a mild word put in place of 'sex'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mild or vague expression substituted for a blunt one is exactly what 'it' is when people mean sex.

clue.text: Yon lass packs mesh bags in the country

blocks.note: a net is a mesh
that girl over there is 'her'
to bag a catch is to land it

explanation.surface: A country girl stuffing string bags with produce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bags' looks like a noun, string bags, but it is a verb, as in landing a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The Netherlands is the European kingdom often called Holland, so it is simply the country meant.

clue.text: Comedians filling with ego on stage

indicators.note: a filling sits inside something else, so the letters lie within the words that follow

blocks.note: the run of letters across these four words

explanation.surface: Stand-up comics filling the stage with their egos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'filling' looks like describing comedians bursting with ego, but it marks the letters inside 'witH EGO ON Stage'. The Goons were Spike Milligan, Peter Sellers and Harry Secombe of BBC radio's The Goon Show.
explanation.definitionFit: The Goons were a famous British radio comedy troupe of the 1950s, so they are comedians collectively.

clue.text: This writer blocks those that could rectify a threat to Troilus

indicators.note: something that blocks a passage sits in the middle of it

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as 'this writer', so me
diodes are rectifiers, turning alternating current into direct

explanation.surface: The writer interfering with people who might fix a danger to the Trojan prince.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rectify' looks like 'set right', but in electronics a rectifier converts alternating current to direct.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida, the Greek Diomedes woos Cressida away, a rival who threatens Troilus in love and battle.

clue.text: Sporting charmer who could make the 11?

blocks.note: first meaning: Harry, the boy wizard who casts charms and plays Quidditch
second meaning: a maker of ceramics, who could produce the china of the 11-across entry

explanation.surface: Could a charming sportsman make the first eleven of a team?
explanation.walkthrough: 'the 11' looks like a cricket or football eleven; it is a cross-reference to 11-across, a set of crockery.
explanation.definitionFit: Harry Potter is the fictional wizard and Quidditch player, while a craftsman throwing clay pots would produce teacups and saucers.

clue.text: A secretive novel set in China

indicators.note: something novel is new, so the letters take a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A mysterious novel whose plot takes place in China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' poses as a book set in China; it is the anagram signal, and 'China' is really lower-case china, porcelain.
explanation.definitionFit: Cups, saucers and teapot made of porcelain together form one matching set of crockery for serving tea.

clue.text: Life drawing is something for evening courses

blocks.note: spirit is life, vitality
players drawing a match are level

explanation.surface: Life drawing as a subject offered at adult evening classes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Life drawing' and 'evening courses' both suggest art classes; 'evening' is making even, and courses are rows of bricks.
explanation.definitionFit: Builders use this bubble tool to check that each course of bricks is laid flat and true, making it even.

clue.text: Way around an ancient land

indicators.note: turning something around makes it face backwards, so its letters read in reverse

blocks.note: a mode is a way or manner

explanation.surface: A route that goes round an old country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way' suggests a road; it is the manner sense, MODE.
explanation.definitionFit: Edom was a biblical kingdom south of the Dead Sea, home of Esau's descendants, so an ancient land.

clue.text: Cool school’s lack of rules

blocks.note: in means fashionable, cool
a school of thought or a field of study is a discipline

explanation.surface: A trendy school where nobody keeps any rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'school' suggests a place of education, but here it is a branch of learning.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiscipline means a failure to keep order or obey rules, which matches lawlessness and an absence of control.

clue.text: Derby’s first alderman translated Utopia

indicators.note: the first of something is its opening letter
translating turns words into a different form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the initial letter of Derby
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Derby councillor producing a translation of Thomas More's Utopia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translated' fits a book like Utopia, written in Latin, but it signals the shuffle. Derby is an English city whose councils once had aldermen.
explanation.definitionFit: Utopia is an imagined ideal place, and a dreamland is likewise a perfect world existing only in fantasy.

clue.text: A deviant, fifty, hiding in a Sarah Waters book

indicators.note: whatever hides something keeps it tucked inside
deviant means departing from the norm, so the letters stray from their order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sexually unorthodox fifty-year-old concealed within one of Sarah Waters's novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fifty' tempts the solver to use the Roman numeral L, but here the word is spelt out in full as fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Affinity (1999) is Sarah Waters's second novel, a Victorian story set in Millbank prison involving a spiritualist medium.

clue.text: Migrant faced timeless moment in a novella

indicators.note: less means without, and time is abbreviated to a single letter that goes
a migrant moves about, so the letters move to new places

blocks.note: taken as written
the word with T, for time, removed
taken as written

explanation.surface: An itinerant worker confronting an eternal instant in a short novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Migrant' looks like the subject of the sentence, and fittingly so, since the book's heroes are migrant ranch hands, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: John Steinbeck's 1937 Of Mice and Men is a short work, longer than a story but shorter than a full novel.

clue.text: O, love a duck!

blocks.note: surface reading: the old exclamation of surprise 'Lor' love a duck!'
setter's reading: a list of three zeros, the letter O, love in tennis and a duck in cricket

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lor' love a duck' is a Cockney exclamation of amazement. Read as a list, the letter O, a love score in tennis and a duck (no runs) in cricket are all zero.
explanation.definitionFit: Each item in the list stands for zero, and nought is the British word for zero, so together they are several of them.

clue.text: Popular Oz character? Absolutely!

blocks.note: in means popular, fashionable
Toto is Dorothy's dog in The Wizard of Oz

explanation.surface: A quiz question about a well-loved Oz character, answered with emphatic agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oz' suggests Australia, but it is L. Frank Baum's land of Oz.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means totally or entirely, the sense of absolutely as 'completely', not as an exclamation of agreement.

clue.text: Juvenile indiscretions, like Larkin’s intros for his prose work

indicators.note: an intro is an opening, so each word contributes only its opening letter

blocks.note: opening letter
opening letter
opening letter
opening letter

explanation.surface: Youthful blunders, such as the poet Larkin's early ventures into fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: Philip Larkin is best known as a poet, but his first novel was Jill (1946), written young, so the surface itself calls it a juvenile indiscretion.
explanation.definitionFit: Larkin published two novels before turning to verse; Jill, set at wartime Oxford, was the first of those fiction books.

clue.text: Story writer’s maiden, cheerful fool, trapped by a soldier

indicators.note: something trapped is held inside whatever caught it

blocks.note: M is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a maiden over
up means in good spirits
an ass is a fool
taken as written
a soldier ant guards the colony

explanation.surface: An author's heroine, cheerful and foolish, caught by a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maiden' suggests a girl, but in cricket a maiden is an over with no runs, abbreviated M on scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: Guy de Maupassant was the French master of the short story, author of 'Boule de Suif' and 'The Necklace'.

clue.text: One forever holding up a mariner’s return

indicators.note: returning means going back the way one came

blocks.note: taken as written
an old salt is a veteran sailor

explanation.surface: Someone eternally delaying a sailor's homecoming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding up' suggests delaying, but it means literally holding something aloft.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Titan Atlas was condemned to bear the heavens on his shoulders for eternity.

clue.text: “What joy is joy, if — be not by” (The Two Gentlemen of Verona)

definitions.text: “What joy is joy, if — be not by” (The Two Gentlemen of Verona)

blocks.clueFragment: “What joy is joy, if — be not by”
blocks.note: a line of verse with a gap, which the missing name fills
the source tells the solver which play's heroine to look for

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: Valentine, banished from Milan, laments being parted from the Duke's daughter he loves.
explanation.definitionFit: Silvia is the heroine Valentine adores in the play; the missing word is her name in his speech in Act 3.

clue.text: American dropped from funny knight’s part in Princess Ida

indicators.note: what is dropped from a group is left out of it

blocks.note: hilarious means very funny
US is short for American
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: An American cut from a comic knight's role in the Gilbert and Sullivan opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Princess Ida is a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera. US is removed from HILARIOUS and N added.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Hilarion is the tenor lead role in Princess Ida, betrothed in infancy to the princess of the title.

clue.text: Man famous for photographing fish

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of the Surrealist photographer whose first name was Man
second meaning: a flat cartilaginous sea fish such as a skate

explanation.surface: A man known for his photographs of fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like a generic person, but it is the photographer's first name, so the definition is his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Man Ray was the American Dada and Surrealist photographer, and the flat-bodied sea creature is also called by this name.

clue.text: Rides around following Jesus in parts of Greece

indicators.note: going around something encloses it

blocks.note: to cycle is to ride a bicycle
AD, Anno Domini, marks the years after Christ's birth

explanation.surface: Pilgrims cycling around Greece in the footsteps of Jesus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following Jesus' suggests discipleship; it means the era dated from his birth.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cyclades are an Aegean island group including Naxos and Mykonos, so they form sections of Greek territory.

clue.text: Macbeth’s servant and armourer agreed about fashion

indicators.note: turned about means facing back the other way

blocks.note: yes signals agreement
ton is an old word for high fashion

explanation.surface: Macbeth's attendant and his armour-maker settled on a matter of style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and armourer' looks like a second person, but it is part of one description; Seyton brings Macbeth his armour in Act 5.
explanation.definitionFit: Seyton is the officer attending Macbeth in the final act, who reports the queen's death and arms him.
